processes: Placing one dot per valence electron around the symbol
Arranging dots on four sides before pairing
Using dot count to predict bonding
plainLanguageExplanation: A Lewis structure is a quick, simple diagram chemists use to show an atom's valence electrons. You write the element's symbol — like Na for sodium — then place dots around it, one dot for each valence electron. Sodium, with one valence electron, gets one dot. Carbon, with four, gets four dots. The dots are placed around the four sides of the symbol, first one per side, then pairing up as needed. Why does this matter? Because the dots reveal bonding. Atoms want full outer shells, so the dots show exactly which electrons are available to bond. An atom with one dot — like sodium — is set up to give that dot away. An atom with seven dots — like chlorine — needs one more. When you draw two symbols next to each other, dots between them can be paired and shared: two symbols sharing a pair of dots are drawing a covalent bond. Lewis structures are the shorthand that lets chemists see, at a glance, how atoms will combine — before a single molecule forms.

whyItMatters: Lewis structures are the everyday tool chemists use to predict bonding before any experiment. Reading a dot diagram tells you how many bonds an atom will form, whether it will give or take electrons, and how molecules will assemble. It is the practical skill that connects valence electrons to real chemical formulas.
didYouKnow: The Lewis structure was invented by Gilbert Lewis in 1916 — over a century later it is still the fastest way chemists picture how atoms bond.
compareReason: A Lewis structure is the valence electron idea drawn as a diagram — comparing the full shell model with the stripped-down dot diagram shows the same idea in two forms.
